mcqs.question: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute actually prevent?
options: Cross-site requests from attaching the cookie
The cookie being sent over plain HTTP
Page scripts reading the cookie through document.cookie
A subdomain from receiving the cookie
mcqs.explanation: HttpOnly makes the cookie inaccessible to page script via document.cookie, removing one exfiltration path for the session identifier. Cross-site sending is governed by SameSite, HTTPS-only transport by Secure, and host scoping by Domain and Path or the `__Host-` prefix. Note the limit, which the other options miss: HttpOnly does not stop an XSS payload from causing authenticated requests while the browser attaches the cookie.

mcqs.question: An API issues stateless JWT access tokens with a 15-minute lifetime plus a rotating refresh token. Product now demands that a demoted admin lose admin access "immediately" and that "sign out everywhere" kill every device at once. A teammate proposes cutting the access-token lifetime to 30 seconds and changing nothing else. What is the accurate assessment?
options: The shorter lifetime only narrows the window a revoked session stays usable; immediacy needs a per-request lookup of server-held state in the access path
A 30-second lifetime is the standard way to implement revocation: no realistic attacker acts inside that window, so shortening the token is the mechanism and the requirement is met
The signature proves the token is authentic, so until `exp` arrives the server has no basis to refuse it; nothing about a JWT can be revoked before its expiry passes
Clearing the token from browser storage on logout is sufficient revocation, because every later request arrives without a credential and is rejected by the server
mcqs.explanation: Revocation is a question about current authority, and a signed token answers only what was true at issuance: `exp` is the one thing that ends its usability, so lifetime controls the window of stale authority and never the ability to close it. A 30-second token still grants 30 seconds of admin after the demotion, and "sign out everywhere" waits out the same window on every device that keeps refreshing — which is why revocation has to live on the refresh path at minimum. Immediacy comes from consulting state per request: a deny-list keyed by `jti`, a per-session version counter checked in the access path, or an opaque session whose row is that state. The strongest distractor is the 30-second lifetime, because it is what most teams actually do and it genuinely cuts exposure — it is a mitigation, not the mechanism, and it buys the smaller window with more refresh traffic. The "signed therefore authoritative" option confuses integrity with freshness: a valid signature says nobody tampered with the claims, not that they are still true. The client-side logout option leaves the token valid for anyone who already copied it. State the cost out loud too: a per-request revocation check reintroduces the store lookup stateless tokens were meant to avoid (RFC 7519 §4.1.4 `exp`, §4.1.7 `jti`: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519#section-4.1.4; OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html).

mcqs.question: Your SPA receives an ID Token from the OIDC provider and sends it to your API as `Authorization: Bearer <id_token>`. The API validates the signature against the provider's JWKS, checks `iss` and `exp`, and returns 200. What is wrong with that?
options: Its audience is the client application, not the API, and it attests an authentication event rather than API access; the API must check `aud` and reject ID Tokens
Nothing: the signature verifies against the provider's published keys, so the caller is provably a user who signed in at that provider, whatever the audience in the token says
Nothing, provided the API also enforces the `scope` claim on the token before serving the request, since scopes are the thing that authorizes API calls on the resource
The lifetime is the only problem: an ID Token expires within minutes, so the API should quietly exchange it for a fresh access token using the refresh token
mcqs.explanation: OIDC returns two tokens addressed to two different recipients: the access token is for the resource server, and the ID Token is for the client — `aud` is the client id, and its claims describe an authentication event (`sub`, `auth_time`, `nonce`). An API that skips the audience check accepts a token minted for a party that was never meant to call it, which is the same hole as accepting a token issued for another service; RFC 9068 requires `aud` validation for JWT access tokens for exactly that reason, and accepting an ID Token also erases the token-class boundary the two-token split exists to create. The strongest distractor is the signature argument, because it is half right: verification proves the provider signed those claims, and nothing in that signature says this API is the intended receiver. The `scope` option fails because scope enforcement only governs a token this API should not be reading at all — an ID Token generally carries no API scope — so it cannot fix audience confusion. The lifetime option names a real annoyance and the wrong remedy: an API holds no refresh token and must never spend one; renewal belongs to the client (OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §3.1.3.7 ID Token Validation: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#IDTokenValidation; RFC 9068 §4: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068.html#section-4).

mcqs.question: A resource server receives a JWT access token. Which set of checks must pass before it may authorize the request?
options: Decoding the payload successfully and confirming that the `exp` claim is still in the future, since a JWT cannot be forged without the signing key
Signature verification with keys from an issuer the API trusts, a pinned algorithm list, and `iss`/`aud`/`exp` checks for this resource server
Signature verification with any key in the shared partner cache, plus the presence of a `sub` claim that names the calling user
Fetching the key from the `jku` URL named in the token header and verifying the signature with whatever key that endpoint returns
mcqs.explanation: A JWT is three base64url segments, and decoding them proves nothing: the payload is readable and writable by anyone, so the first step is signature verification against a key belonging to an issuer this API has configured. Algorithm pinning belongs in the same step — accepting the header's `alg` on its own is how unsigned tokens and HS256-signed-with-the-public-key forgeries get in — and RFC 9068 then requires `iss` and `aud` to be checked so a token minted for another service or tenant is refused. The strongest distractor is the decode-and-`exp` option, because it looks like validation and it is the shape of bug that ships: an unsigned `{"sub":"admin","exp":9999999999}` passes it. The `jku` option is the sophisticated-looking one and the more dangerous: a key URL inside the token is chosen by whoever wrote the token, so the verifier confirms the attacker's signature with the attacker's key and makes an outbound request they control; key location comes from configuration, never from the token (RFC 8725: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725.html; RFC 9068 §4: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068.html#section-4). The shared-cache option verifies a signature and still accepts any partner whose key is cached, and `sub` is neither authorization nor evidence of audience.

mcqs.question: In the authorization code flow with PKCE for a browser SPA, what does the code verifier specifically prevent?
options: Nothing about the code being visible in the redirect: it makes an intercepted code useless, because the token endpoint demands the verifier behind the challenge
It protects the access token, since the API validates the verifier and rejects any token that was minted for a different client application
It stops an attacker from substituting the authorization response in the victim's browser by binding the returned callback to the browser session that started the login flow
It encrypts the authorization code in the redirect URI, so intermediaries, proxies and logs cannot read it or replay it within its lifetime
mcqs.explanation: PKCE binds redemption to the party that started the flow: the client sends `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))` with the authorization request and presents the raw verifier only at the token endpoint, so an authorization code observed on the way back — a hijacked custom scheme, a leaked URL, an app registered for the same redirect — cannot be exchanged by anyone who does not hold the verifier. That is proof of possession at one endpoint, not encryption and not client authentication. The strongest distractor is the response-substitution option, because PKCE and `state` are routinely conflated: `state` binds the returned response to the browser session that began the flow (login CSRF and response mix-up), while PKCE says nothing about which browser received the response. The verifier-at-the-API option confuses the two jobs: the verifier is never sent to the resource server, which validates the signature and audience of the access token, and a public client has no secret for PKCE to replace. The encryption option is simply false: the code still travels in the URL, which is why exact redirect URIs, referrer policy and log scrubbing still matter (RFC 7636 §1 and §4.1: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636#section-1).

mcqs.question: A live credential is discovered in a public repository's history. What is the correct first response?
options: Delete the file, force-push the branch so the commit disappears from history, and close the finding as remediated
Add the path to .gitignore and re-commit, so the value never appears in any future history of the repository
Revoke or rotate the credential immediately, audit what it reached, and treat every copy in history as live
Rename the variable and obfuscate the value in the next release so scanners stop flagging the file
mcqs.explanation: A committed secret must be treated as exposed the moment it landed in git: clones, forks, CI caches and archives keep the old commit, so the only control that ends the exposure is revocation or rotation, followed by auditing what the credential reached. The strongest distractor is the force-push, because it feels like removal: rewriting history hides the value from the default branch but revokes nothing, and everyone who cloned has it. `.gitignore` prevents future commits of that path and does nothing for the value already published, and renaming or obfuscating changes the string a scanner matches, not who can use it — scanners are detection, not the control. Order matters: revoke first, because audit and remediation take hours and the credential is live through all of them; scrub history afterwards as compliance hygiene (OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html).

mcqs.question: A login validates the password, then shows a TOTP step. The service issues the session cookie at the password step and stores `mfaPending: true` on the server-side session row; middleware rejects requests while that flag is set. What is the structural flaw?
options: Nothing structural: the flag lives on the server-side session and cannot be forged by the client, so the session is unusable until the second factor passes
The pending window is too long; give that session a five-minute lifetime and extend it when the TOTP code verifies

The session already exists after one factor, so every consumer of it — routes, sockets, older API versions, workers — must remember the flag; a separate short-lived pending-login record, with the session minted only after the factor verifies, inverts the default
TOTP verification should happen in the browser so the server never creates a session before the code is checked
mcqs.explanation: The flaw is the default, not forgeability. With the flag design the user holds an authenticated session after one factor, and the second factor becomes a condition every consumer has to remember: a websocket upgrade, a GraphQL resolver, a legacy API route, a background job that trusts `session.userId`. One omission is a full authentication bypass with only the password, and it fails silently because the session looks valid everywhere else. A pending-login record reverses that: the post-password capability can complete exactly one thing, and `issueSession` sits behind the successful factor check. The strongest distractor is the forged-flag objection, because signing or server-storing the flag genuinely stops tampering — which is why the pattern survives review — but it does not put the single-factor state behind a check. A five-minute lifetime narrows the exposure without changing which state exists, and client-side verification hands the seed and the expected code to the attacker's browser. Either design also needs per-user attempt limits and an atomically recorded last accepted time step, so a captured code cannot be replayed inside its window (OWASP Multifactor Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html; RFC 6238 §5.2: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238#section-5.2).

mcqs.question: A reset handler loads the token row, returns 400 when `usedAt` is already set, hashes the new password (~250 ms with bcrypt), then marks the token used and stores the hash. Two requests carrying the same still-valid token arrive milliseconds apart with different passwords. What happens?
options: Only one request succeeds: the second mark-used UPDATE waits on the first one's row lock and then observes `usedAt` set

Both requests pass the `usedAt` check before either write commits, so both can set a password; the token must be claimed first with one conditional statement — `UPDATE ... SET used_at = now() WHERE digest = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now() RETURNING user_id` — and only the winner proceeds
Both succeed and the last write wins, which is acceptable because the link was only ever sent to the account owner
Wrapping the read and the writes in one transaction at the database's default isolation level makes the pair atomic, so the loser fails cleanly
mcqs.explanation: `SELECT then UPDATE` is two statements, and the gap between them is exactly where both requests live: nothing forces the write to re-test the read, so the bcrypt delay only makes the race wider and the slower password becomes the stored one. The fix is a compare-and-set — a conditional UPDATE (or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction) that claims the row, `RETURNING` the user id, and lets only the winner hash and write. The strongest distractor is the transaction option, because it is the answer a senior engineer gives before checking the isolation semantics: grouping statements in a transaction is atomicity, not serialization of a read-then-write. At the default isolation the second transaction's SELECT returns the same snapshot and its UPDATE re-applies to the row once the lock clears, so both writes land; only an explicit predicate or an explicit locking or isolation choice closes the window. The last-write-wins option confuses possession with exclusivity — links get forwarded, archived and fetched by mail scanners — and single use exists precisely so a leaked copy stops working; with last-write-wins an attacker who races the victim ends up owning the password. The row-lock option fails for the same reason as the transaction one: the lock serializes the writes, but the loser's UPDATE carries no `used_at IS NULL` condition to fail (OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.html).

scenarios.prompt: This middleware guards every API route. A pen test got a 200 from `GET /v1/orders` using a token minted by a partner issuer that should only reach its own endpoints. Review the code, name every validation flaw, and describe the correct order of operations.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
The symptom you were handed is the audience hole: the middleware resolves a key from `payload.iss` in a shared multi-partner cache and then never checks that the token was issued for this API. Any issuer already in that cache produces a signature that verifies, and with no `aud` check and no per-API issuer allowlist the request reaches `/v1/orders`. The same gap admits an ID Token, whose audience is a client, as an API credential.

Underneath the symptom, the ordering is inverted. `jwt.decode` runs first and its unverified `iss` chooses the key, so whoever wrote the token chooses which key gets tried; the point of verification is that the choice comes from configuration, not from the header. The decoded object also fills `req.user`, which is the wrong habit even when the signature later succeeds — authorization state is built from the verified result only.

The algorithm list is a policy bug: `['none', 'HS256', 'RS256']` declares unsigned tokens acceptable. With this library and a key supplied, an `alg: none` token fails the signature comparison, so this exact line is not exploitable today — do not rely on that. The allowlist is the service's statement of what it accepts, one refactor that omits the key turns it into a bypass, and nothing in the code says `none` is unacceptable. Mixing HS256 with RS256 in one list is separately exploitable: if a partner's cached entry is an RSA public key, an attacker HMAC-signs using that public key as the secret and the same key verifies the result — algorithm confusion.

Then the checks that do exist are the wrong ones. `if (Date.now() / 1000 < verified.exp)` is a hand-rolled expiry test: it never looks at `nbf`, ignores clock skew, and rejects a token with no `exp` only because `undefined` compares false. Required claims belong to the verifier (`requiredClaims`, `maxTokenAge`) instead of being reconstructed by hand.

Correct order of operations, per the JWT profile for OAuth 2.0 access tokens (RFC 9068: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068.html): resolve the expected issuer for this route from configuration; fetch keys only from that issuer's JWKS, selecting by `kid`; verify with one pinned algorithm family and no `none`; validate `iss` against the allowlist, `aud` against this API, `exp`/`nbf` with tolerance, and any required claims; build `req.user` from the verified payload; and keep endpoint authorization — may this subject perform this action on this resource — as a separate check after authentication. Refuse a token whose `typ` marks it as an ID Token rather than an access token.
rubric: Identifies decode-before-verify as trusting unverified claims — `iss` included — to choose the key, and notes that `req.user` is also built from the decoded object

Flags `none` in the algorithm allowlist as a policy that accepts unsigned tokens without overstating what this library does today, and the HS256/RS256 mix as algorithm confusion against a cached public key
Explains the reported symptom: no per-API issuer allowlist and no `aud` check, so any partner issuer in the cache is accepted, ID Tokens included
Replaces the hand-rolled `exp` comparison with required claims and clock-skew-aware validation
States the order explicitly — configured issuer, that issuer's JWKS by `kid`, pinned algorithm, then `iss`/`aud`/`exp` — and keeps endpoint scope policy separate

scenarios.prompt: A penetration test reports that an attacker can log in as a victim whose session identifier was planted beforehand. Review this login and promotion flow, explain the vulnerability, and fix it.
rubric: Identifies session fixation: the client-supplied sid survives authentication instead of being regenerated
Requires rotation after privilege changes, not only at login, plus invalidation of the old identifier
Questions SameSite=None, preferring Lax or Strict unless a documented cross-site need exists
Adds server-side session hygiene: expiration, invalidation at logout, and login rate limiting
Recognizes that TLS and Secure cookies do not prevent fixation, since the attack concerns identifier provenance

scenarios.prompt: An interviewer hands you this complete password reset flow and asks for a review focused on enumeration, token handling and sessions. Find every gap, name the attack each one enables, and rewrite the flow.
rubric: Catches enumeration beyond the status code — the echoed `sentTo`, the 404, and the timing gap between the mail-sending branch and the early return — and prescribes one constant response, comparable work (queued mail instead of a quick exit), and per-account rate limits
Flags that the link is built from `req.headers.host` over plain HTTP and requires a configured canonical HTTPS origin (or a validated trusted-domain list), plus no-referrer on the reset page
Requires storing a digest rather than the raw token, binding it to its purpose, and checking expiry at redemption instead of trusting a long TTL
Demands atomic single-use consumption — a conditional update or locked claim — and explains the check-then-write race rather than assuming a transaction fixes it
Removes the auto-login and invalidates existing sessions and other outstanding reset tokens after the password change, keeping the normal password policy and a notification to the owner
